sketch: The debate assumes that if there's first-person authority, it extends to our beliefs and intentions generally. But the confabulation literature shows that when asked about our standing attitudes ('Do I believe in gun control?'), we often generate an answer through the same interpretive process observers use—except observers see our patterns better because they aren't inside our motivated reasoning. The real asymmetry is occurrent: when I judge right now that gun control is good, that very act of judging constitutes an attitude-in-the-moment that only I can report non-interpretively. This explains both the phenomenology of authority (we feel authoritative when forming judgments, not when reporting pre-existing beliefs) and the data (we confabulate about standing attitudes but not about what we're currently thinking). Moran gets closest to this with his emphasis on the deliberative stance, but still treats it as revealing pre-existing attitudes rather than constituting momentary ones.

outlines.surprise: The standard debate assumes first-person authority must concern persisting attitudes to be philosophically interesting, treating occurrent states as too thin to matter. This outline makes the occurrent-standing distinction the central explanatory posit, treating what seemed peripheral as fundamental and inverting what seemed obvious about standing attitudes.
outlines.commitment: The outline commits to the claim that observers genuinely know our standing attitudes better than we do—not just 'sometimes' or 'in some respects' but systematically and structurally. A cautious version would say we and others have 'different' or 'complementary' access; this says others have superior access where it matters.

divergence.sharpest: Whether to lead with the occurrent/standing distinction itself or with the standing-attitude half of the inversion. Leading with the distinction (outlines 0, 2, 4) frames the paper as discovering that a familiar category divides into two with opposite epistemic profiles. Leading with third-person superiority on standing attitudes (outlines 1, 3, 5) frames the paper as inverting received wisdom about self-knowledge, with the occurrent domain emerging as the residual space of first-person authority. This determines whether readers experience the thesis as 'the traditional debate was asking about the wrong thing' versus 'the traditional answer was backwards.'
divergence.absent: None of the outlines includes a section defending the functional-dispositional conception of standing attitudes against alternatives (like standing attitudes as stored representations or as higher-order dispositions to form occurrent judgments). This conception is load-bearing—if standing attitudes were introspectable mental states rather than behavioral patterns, the third-person superiority claim would fail—but every outline treats it as established in passing rather than argued for.

addresses.text: Alex Byrne's transparency account (in 'Transparency and Self-Knowledge', 2005) which treats belief self-attribution as uniform—both standing beliefs and occurrent judgments are accessed by answering the world-directed question—collapsing the distinction the section draws.

Alex Byrne's transparency account in 'Transparency and Self-Knowledge' (2005) treats 'Do I believe that p?' and 'Is p true?' as answerable by the same procedure for both standing and occurrent attitudes, denying that occurrent acts have special epistemic status

Daniel Dennett's position in 'The Logical Geography of Computational Approaches' (1986) and related works that all mental states, including occurrent thoughts, are constituted by functional patterns observable in principle from the third-person perspective—though Dennett might grant practical inaccessibility at the moment of occurrence
David Armstrong's 'Belief, Truth and Knowledge' (1973) view that beliefs are categorical mental states directly accessible to introspection, not dispositions
David Chalmers' view in 'The Contents of Consciousness' that dispositional beliefs are stored contentful states that remain present but non-conscious, not merely patterns of behavior and inference.
David Hume's bundle theory as defended by Galen Strawson in 'The Self and the SESMET' (2011), which denies psychological continuity requires dispositional states beyond sequences of token experiences

Dorit Bar-On's neo-expressivist view holds that the phenomenology of authority accompanies all spontaneous avowals regardless of whether they concern occurrent or standing states, because authority derives from the expressive rather than reportive character of avowal (Speaking My Mind, 2004)

Dorit Bar-On's view in 'Speaking My Mind' that even if self-knowledge involves some interpretation, the subject's access to their own reasons, memories, and current phenomenology gives them interpretive advantages that outweigh any motivational bias.
Eric Schwitzgebel's 'Perplexities of Consciousness' (2011) position that introspection is unreliable even for current experiences and occurrent thoughts

Eric Schwitzgebel's argument in 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' (2008) shows self-reports of standing attitudes are systematically unreliable, but he concludes introspection itself is unreliable rather than that self-reports are interpretive

Eric Schwitzgebel's position in 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' (2008) argues for symmetry of unreliability but does not grant others superior access—he claims both self- and other-ascription are highly unreliable for standing attitudes, whereas the present claim is that others are systematically better interpreters

Eric Schwitzgebel's skepticism about introspection holds that we have no better access to our current conscious states than to our dispositional ones, and that introspective reports about current experience are as unreliable as reports about standing attitudes (Perplexities of Consciousness, 2011)

Eric Schwitzgebel's skepticism about self-knowledge ('Perplexities of Consciousness', 2011, and 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection', 2008) acknowledges poor first-person access to many mental states but does not claim others have superior access—he treats it as general epistemic difficulty rather than an asymmetry favoring the third person, which would refute the directional superiority claim.

Eric Schwitzgebel's view in 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' treats memory and phenomenology as direct access to psychological facts rather than as evidence requiring interpretation, even while arguing such access is unreliable.
Gareth Evans' 'The Varieties of Reference' (1982) transparency account that treats first-person authority as extending to beliefs generally, not just occurrent judgments

Moran's own position in 'Authority and Estrangement' (2001) where he argues that answering 'Do I believe that P?' from the deliberative stance (considering whether P is true) does reveal one's standing belief about P, not merely an occurrent judgment—the authority of the deliberative stance is supposed to extend to standing attitudes precisely because deliberation determines what one believes

Peter Carruthers' interpretive sensory-access theory ('The Opacity of Mind', 2011) which argues that even seemingly immediate self-knowledge of current thoughts involves interpretation of inner speech and imagery through the same mindreading mechanisms we use for others, denying privileged access even to occurrent states.

Peter Carruthers' view in 'The Opacity of Mind' that all self-knowledge is interpretive and that subjects have no privileged access even to occurrent mental states, which are accessed through the same mindreading mechanisms used for others.

Peter Carruthers's interpretive sensory-access theory holds that confabulation reflects the same interpretive process for both occurrent and standing states, with apparent differences explained by differential salience of sensory evidence rather than a categorical distinction in access (The Opacity of Mind, 2011)

Richard Moran's 'Authority and Estrangement' (2001) explains first-person authority through the deliberative stance but treats deliberation as revealing pre-existing standing attitudes rather than constituting occurrent judgments, thus failing to predict observer superiority for standing attitudes

Richard Moran's 'Authority and Estrangement' (2001) maintains first-person authority through the deliberative stance—answering whether I believe P by answering whether P—but treats this as revealing standing attitudes rather than constituting occurrent ones, thus preserving traditional first-person superiority across both standing and occurrent attitudes and rejecting the inversion.
Richard Moran's 'Authority and Estrangement' (2001) where transparency is presented as a way of accessing what one believes (standing attitude) rather than only what one is judging now

Richard Moran's deliberative approach holds that the evidence distinctively available to subjects (their reasons and deliberative processes) reveals their attitudes directly rather than requiring interpretation (Authority and Estrangement, 2001)

Richard Moran's position in 'Authority and Estrangement' (2001) that first-person authority stems from the deliberative stance—reasoning about what to believe rather than introspecting what one believes—which suggests the phenomenology of authority comes from active rational engagement, not from privileged evidence access

Richard Moran's view in 'Authority and Estrangement' that the deliberative stance reveals our standing attitudes by making transparent what we already believe, rather than the avowal constituting a new momentary attitude.
Sydney Shoemaker's 'First-Person Access' (1994) view that the phenomenology of authority accompanies introspection of standing beliefs just as much as current thoughts

Sydney Shoemaker's constitutivism holds that self-ascriptions of belief are made true by the very act of sincere self-ascription without requiring evidence or interpretation (Self-Knowledge and Self-Identity, 1963)

Sydney Shoemaker's functionalist account (in 'Self-Knowledge and Self-Identity', 1963, and later work) which grants that mental states are functional dispositions but maintains we have special introspective access to our own dispositional states through a self-monitoring mechanism unavailable to others.

Sydney Shoemaker's position in 'On Knowing One's Own Mind' (1988) that self-knowledge is primarily about current conscious states, not standing attitudes—though even Shoemaker treats conscious access to standing beliefs as unproblematic when they are 'before the mind'

Sydney Shoemaker's transparency account in 'Self-Knowledge and Self-Identity' (1963) holds that first-person authority extends to standing beliefs because the subject has constitutive authority over their attitudes, which would entail subjects cannot be systematically worse than observers at identifying them
Sydney Shoemaker's view in 'Self-Knowledge and Self-Identity' that self-knowledge of beliefs involves a direct rational connection to those beliefs rather than inference from evidence.

Tamar Gendler's alief framework ('Alief and Belief', 2008) explains confabulation through belief-alief conflicts without requiring different asymmetries for different mental state types—we confabulate when reporting beliefs that conflict with aliefs, but both observers and subjects face similar epistemic problems, preserving symmetry and refuting the need for inversion.

Tamar Szabó Gendler's position in 'Alief and Belief' (2008) that conscious judgments often fail to capture our genuine attitudes (which may be carried by aliefs), implying that even occurrent avowals are interpretations rather than constitutive expressions—though Gendler focuses on standing aliefs rather than denying occurrent authority per se

Tania Lombrozo and Alison Gopnik's work on self-knowledge as theory ('The Causal Theory of Self-Knowledge', unpublished circulated manuscript) argues that self-attribution involves the same causal-explanatory framework we use for others, just with different evidence—suggesting no categorical non-interpretive access even to occurrent states, only different data inputs to the same interpretive mechanism.

The constitutive view defended by Crispin Wright and others holds that avowals have their special status because they partly constitute the standing attitudes they report, thus preserving first-person authority for standing attitudes while explaining confabulation as performance error (Rails to Infinity, 2001)

The fundamental attribution error literature (Ross 1977, Gilbert & Malone 1995) which shows observers systematically over-attribute behavior to dispositions rather than situations, suggesting observers might be worse interpreters of standing attitudes than the agent.
Timothy Wilson's 'Strangers to Ourselves' (2002) interpretation that confabulation studies reveal pervasive self-ignorance across all domains of mental life

Traditional first-person authority defenders like Donald Davidson in 'First Person Authority' (1984) hold that self-knowledge of propositional attitudes generally has special epistemic status regardless of the standing/occurrent distinction, which would be false if the asymmetry inverts along that distinction
Tyler Burge's 'Our Entitlement to Self-Knowledge' (1996) view that we have a priori warrant for self-knowledge of content-bearing attitudes based on privileged internal access

Tyler Burge's position in 'Our Entitlement to Self-Knowledge' (1996) that we have a constitutive rational entitlement to self-knowledge of our standing propositional attitudes because critical reasoning presupposes such knowledge—this would refute the inversion by establishing first-person authority over standing attitudes as a rational necessity

Tyler Burge's preservationist view holds that memory preserves first-person authority about one's past beliefs and intentions, giving subjects superior access to their own standing attitudes through recollection (Content Preservation, 1993)
